meta.reviewer_notes: The analogy is tested item by item, which makes each individual defect available as a wrong answer to the main idea question, and the third paragraph's insistence that the error is directional rather than random is the sentence that kills the option about unpredictable variation. The fourth paragraph does two opposite things with one fact, which is where the relationship question lives, and readers who take it as a rescue of the analogy misread the whole close. 2026-10-03 CAT-size pass: 655→514 words, 5→5 paragraphs, 5→4 questions. No paragraph dropped, since the figure, the four-item test, the direction of the bias, the double use of migration and the relocated defence are each one step, and the relationship question names the third and fourth paragraphs in its options; tightened each, folding the laboratory's four items into one sentence. Dropped q3 (vocabulary in context, the least CAT-like of the five); difficulty set to medium (6), in line with the corpus's comparable analogy-driven arguments.
meta.tone: sceptical, orderly, warmer at the close

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option gathering two of the three defects, which are named in a single paragraph and leaves the whole of the last two paragraphs, where the analogy is broken and the defence relocated, with nothing to do. Q2's rival is the option about results varying unpredictably, which the third paragraph forecloses by saying the stream of results is not merely noisy but encouraging, the defects all pushing the same way. Q3's rival is the option about something offered freely without expectation of return, which is the word's commonest sense and not the sense the sentence needs, since it is opposed to assigned and explained by the province that has the machinery and the officials and the conditions. Q4's rival is the option that the fourth paragraph withdraws the criticism, which mistakes the second half of a two-sided observation for a retraction; the paragraph calls migration a further wound before calling it the one thing a laboratory cannot offer. Q5's rival is the option naming knowledge as the strongest case for federalism, which is the position the final paragraph says has been made in the wrong language for two centuries. (2026-10-03, CAT-size pass: q3 was dropped, so any note above about it no longer applies.)

paragraphs.text: The most attractive thing ever said in defence of a federal constitution is that it turns a country into a set of laboratories. A measure nobody has tried can be tried in one province: if it works, the others copy it; if it fails, the failure is contained, and the country has still learned something. The figure has done a great deal of political work and deserves to be checked rather than admired.

A laboratory supplies four things: variation the experimenter chooses, so that which unit receives which treatment carries no information about the unit; subjects who stay in the condition they were put in; a common instrument, so that results mean the same everywhere; and publication of the failures, which is the least glamorous of the four and does most of the work, since an inference drawn from successes alone is not an inference. Now set the federal case against the list. The variation is volunteered, not assigned: the province that takes up a novel measure is typically the one with the machinery to run it, officials who believe in it and conditions that suit it. The measurement is taken by the government that adopted the policy and staked something on it. And the failures are quietly discontinued, not published.

So the arrangement is a poor instrument of inference, and it fails in one direction rather than at random. Self-selection puts policies where they were likeliest to succeed; interested measurement records the success generously; silent discontinuation takes the counter-examples out of view. The stream of results is therefore not merely noisy. It is encouraging, and it would go on being encouraging if every one of the policies were worthless.

The remaining item on the list is the one that matters, because no better practice could repair it. Subjects in a laboratory do not move between the conditions. People do. A province with a generous provision attracts the people who need it, one with a severe provision loses them, and much of what looks like a policy's effect is the arrival and departure of the people it was measured on. That is a further wound to the comparison. It is also, at the same time, the one thing in the whole arrangement that a laboratory cannot offer, since movement is a verdict delivered by the subjects themselves, which no department can record generously.

Which suggests that the defence has been conducted in the wrong language for two hundred years. The case for letting provinces differ is not that the country finds out what works, because on this evidence it does not. It is that a population which disagrees about something irreconcilable can live under two answers instead of one, without either side having to be beaten. That is a considerable good, and it has nothing to do with knowledge. It also sits badly beside the first. The more freely people move to the arrangement that suits them, the better the federation works as a settlement and the worse as an experiment, so an argument claiming both goods claims more than the arrangement can give.

questions.target_mistake: taking one of the three defects listed in a single paragraph as the passage's point, and leaving the relocation of the defence unexplained
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say before looking: bad as an experiment, good as a settlement, and the second improves as the first gets worse.
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Federal systems learn much less from policy variation than they suppose, because failures go unpublished and successes are self-reported.
options.B: Federal variation is a poor way to learn what works and a good way to let disagreement survive, and the two pull apart.
options.C: Because people can move between jurisdictions, a comparison between two of them is not worth the making.
options.D: The laboratory analogy should be abandoned, since a federation lacks the controls that a laboratory has.

explanation.expert_notice: The last paragraph states the verdict in two halves and then sets them against each other: the country does not find out what works, the arrangement lets two answers coexist without either side being beaten, and the more freely people move the better it works as a settlement and the worse as an experiment.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries both halves and the tension between them, which is what the passage's own shape requires. The second and third paragraphs earn the first half by testing the analogy item by item, the fourth supplies the movement that both spoils the comparison and delivers the verdict, and the fifth converts all of it into a defence of a different kind. An option that names only a defect leaves two paragraphs with nothing to do.
explanation.question_type_note: In a passage built on an analogy, the main idea is usually where the analogy breaks and what the author puts in its place. Test each candidate by asking which paragraphs it makes redundant.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author lists several faults in one paragraph and then writes two more paragraphs, the faults are not the point. Look for the sentence that says what the thing is good for instead.

distractors.why_wrong: Two of the three defects named in the third paragraph are gathered here, and all three of them are preliminary to the fourth difference and to the relocation of the defence in the last paragraph.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the defect the passage praises most warmly, calling publication of failures the item that does most of the work, so a reader ranks it as the main charge.

distractors.why_wrong: The analogy is not given up; it is worked through to the point where it breaks, and the break is what yields the passage's positive claim. The fourth paragraph treats the difference it finds as the one that matters precisely because it is not a failure of control that better practice could mend.
distractors.seductive_element: The second and third paragraphs are so thoroughly deflationary that abandonment feels like where they must be heading, and the recommendation is stated in the confident register of a conclusion.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph calls migration a further wound to the comparison, which is a matter of degree; converting that into a comparison that can never be trusted at all states something the passage is careful not to say, and drops the second and more important thing migration is said to do.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because movement between jurisdictions really is the difference the author calls the one that matters, so the option looks as though it has identified the passage's central point.

questions.target_mistake: reading three systematic defects as a source of noise, when the passage says all three push the same way
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will name a direction, since the paragraph insists the failure is directional rather than random.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that the results produced by federal policy variation will tend to

options.A: be too few in number to support any general conclusion about a policy's effects
options.B: run in a favourable direction, since a policy is tried where it was likeliest to work
options.C: vary unpredictably, since no two jurisdictions are ever quite alike in their conditions
options.D: understate a policy's benefits, since the unit that tries it carries the whole cost

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph states the direction and then explains it three times over. Self-selection puts policies where they were likeliest to succeed, interested measurement records the success generously, and silent discontinuation removes the counter-examples, so the stream of results is not merely noisy but encouraging.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that conclusion in the form of a tendency, with the first of the three mechanisms attached. The inference is forced rather than merely available, because the paragraph ends by saying the results would go on being encouraging even if every policy were worthless, which is a statement about a bias and not about scatter.
explanation.question_type_note: When a passage lists several defects, ask whether they point the same way. A set of biases that reinforce one another supports a very different inference from a set that cancels out.
explanation.reading_habit: Distinguish noise from bias whenever a passage criticises a source of evidence. Noise makes results useless in both directions; bias makes them useful only to somebody who knows which way it runs.

distractors.why_wrong: The number of trials is never discussed, and the passage's complaint would survive any number of them, since each additional case is produced by the same three mechanisms. A thousand self-selected, self-measured, quietly abandoned trials would be as encouraging as ten.
distractors.seductive_element: Small samples are the standard objection to any claim built on a handful of cases, and readers supply the objection they already know.

distractors.why_wrong: The bias runs the other way. The measurement is said to be taken by the government that adopted the policy and staked something on it, which is offered as a reason for expecting success to be recorded generously rather than grudgingly.
distractors.seductive_element: A province that bears a failure alone does sound like one with a grievance, and readers who notice that the failure is contained there while the whole country learns attach a motive to it.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage grants that jurisdictions differ and insists that the resulting error is systematic. Its exact words are that the stream of results is not merely noisy, which sets aside unpredictability in order to name the direction instead.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because differences between jurisdictions really are the passage's subject, and unpredictability is the conclusion a reader draws from differences without asking which way they lean.

questions.target_mistake: reading the second half of the fourth paragraph as a retraction of the criticism rather than as a second use of the same fact
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: this paragraph adds one more difference, and that difference does two opposite jobs at once.
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the relation of the fourth paragraph to the third?

options.A: The fourth names a further difference that worsens the third's verdict and is then put to a second use.
options.B: The fourth withdraws the criticism made in the third and restores the analogy.
options.C: The fourth restates the third's objection more strongly and draws a practical conclusion.
options.D: The fourth supplies the evidence for the verdict the third had merely asserted.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph uses one fact twice, and says so in consecutive sentences. Migration is called a further wound to the comparison, and then, at the same time, the one thing in the whole arrangement that a laboratory cannot offer, since it is a verdict delivered by the subjects themselves.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps both uses, which is what the paragraph requires and what the last paragraph then depends on. The difference deepens the third paragraph's verdict, because the effect of a policy is now confounded by who arrived and who left; and it simultaneously produces the good the passage ends by defending, which has nothing to do with knowledge. Reading the paragraph as either a rescue or a further complaint discards half of it.
explanation.question_type_note: A relationship question asks what one part does to another. Where a paragraph uses a single fact for two purposes, the answer has to carry both, and options that carry one are the near-misses.
explanation.reading_habit: Watch for the phrase at the same time. Authors use it to mark a fact that cuts both ways, and a question is nearly always waiting on whichever half the reader dropped.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph was not short of evidence; it named three mechanisms and said how each pushed the verdict in the same direction. The fourth introduces something the third had not mentioned at all, and calls it a difference rather than a demonstration.
distractors.seductive_element: A paragraph that follows a strong verdict does usually support it, and migration is concrete in a way the previous paragraph's abstractions were not.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph opens by calling migration a fourth difference and a wound to the comparison, which is criticism added rather than criticism taken back. What follows is not a defence of the analogy but the discovery of a good the analogy could never have named.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the paragraph does turn warm halfway through, and a reader who meets praise after two paragraphs of complaint reads it as a change of mind.

distractors.why_wrong: The objection is not restated but extended, since movement between conditions is a new item and the only one the author says better practice could not repair. No practical conclusion is drawn here either; the practical work is done in the final paragraph, and it concerns how the defence should be worded rather than what anyone should do.
distractors.seductive_element: The paragraph does intensify the case against the analogy, and readers who catch the intensification supply a conclusion because arguments usually end in one.

questions.target_mistake: converting the author's valuing of published failures into the recommendation he pointedly declines to make
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will be something the author asserts about what makes an inference possible, rather than about what a federation ought to do.
questions.stem: With which of the following would the author be most likely to agree?

options.A: A federation's provinces ought to publish their failures, which would make the comparison sound.
options.B: Publishing failures matters more to an inference than controlling who gets the treatment.
options.C: The strongest case for federalism is the knowledge that policy variation produces.
options.D: A policy that has worked in one province will generally work in a similar one.

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph does not merely list the four things a laboratory supplies; it ranks them. Publication of the failures is called the least glamorous of the four and the one that does most of the work, and the reason is given in the same sentence, since an inference drawn from successes alone is not an inference.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that ranking put as a comparison. The author places publication above the other three items, one of which is precisely the experimenter's control over which unit receives which treatment, and he gives his ground in the same sentence, since successes on their own support no conclusion whatever. The third paragraph then shows the ranking at work, because it is silent discontinuation that keeps the stream of results encouraging however worthless the policies were.
explanation.question_type_note: An agree-question is settled by what the author asserts in his own voice, and by what his argument would collapse without. Ask which option he needs, not merely which he might accept.
explanation.reading_habit: When a passage demolishes the usual justification for something and then keeps defending it, find the sentence naming the new kind of justification. That sentence is what the author must believe.

distractors.why_wrong: Both halves fail. The author values published failures highly and still recommends nothing, naming publication in the course of a diagnosis rather than a programme; and the fourth paragraph rules out the repair, since the difference that matters is expressly not a defect better practice could mend, so no amount of publishing would make the comparison sound.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the author really does rate publication above everything else on the list, and a defect named that pointedly invites the repair.

distractors.why_wrong: The whole argument of the third paragraph is against inferring anything of the kind, since policies are adopted where they were likeliest to work and success is recorded by the party that staked something on it. A similar province is exactly the case where self-selection has already done its work.
distractors.seductive_element: Copying what worked elsewhere is the practical hope the laboratory image was built to support, and the qualification about similar conditions sounds like the caution the passage has been urging.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the defence the last paragraph says has been conducted in the wrong language for two hundred years, and the same paragraph denies its premise by stating that the country does not find out what works. The author's case rests on something he says has nothing to do with knowledge.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is the position the passage spends most of its length discussing, and prolonged attention is easily mistaken for endorsement.

vocabulary.passage_use: The variation is volunteered, not assigned
vocabulary.meaning_here: taken up by the unit itself rather than allotted to it

vocabulary.passage_use: a population which disagrees about something irreconcilable
vocabulary.meaning_here: incapable of being settled by agreement between the parties

vocabulary.passage_use: silent discontinuation takes the counter-examples out of view
vocabulary.meaning_here: the stopping of a programme without any announcement
kept from spreading beyond the place it occurred

mentor.challenge: A famous image is tested against what the thing it compares to actually does. Watch the fourth paragraph closely, because the fact it introduces is used twice, in opposite directions, and readers who take the second use for a change of mind lose the ending.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: The figure of a federation as a set of laboratories fails on three of the four things a laboratory supplies, and fails in one direction rather than at random, so the results such a system produces would be encouraging even if every policy were worthless; and the remaining item on the list, that people move between jurisdictions, both wounds the comparison further and supplies a verdict no laboratory can obtain, which means the case for letting provinces differ is that irreconcilable disagreement can survive under two answers rather than that anybody learns anything, and the two goods pull against each other.
mentor.main_idea: Federal variation is defended as a way of finding out what works. Measured against a laboratory it fails three tests at once, and all three failures push the same way, so the record of results is systematically encouraging. The one remaining difference, that people move, spoils the comparison further while delivering something no experiment can: the subjects' own judgement. So the honest defence of federalism is that it lets people who disagree live under different answers, and the freer the movement, the better that works and the worse the experiment does.
mentor.simple_explanation:
The nicest thing anybody ever said in favour of a federal country is that it turns the place into a set of laboratories. Nobody knows whether a new policy works, so let one province try it. If it works, everyone copies. If it fails, only one province has paid for the failure.

The author says the image deserves to be checked rather than admired, so he checks it.

What does a real laboratory give you? Four things. The experimenter decides which unit gets which treatment, so the choice tells you nothing about the unit. The subjects stay in whichever condition they were put into. Everyone measures with the same instrument, so a result here means what a result there means. And failures get published, which is the dullest of the four and does the most work, because a conclusion drawn only from successes is not a conclusion at all.

Now look at a federation. The province that tries a new policy chose to try it, and it is typically the province with the right machinery, officials who believe in it, and local conditions that suit it. The measuring is done by the government that adopted the policy and has its reputation in it. And failures are never published; they are just quietly dropped.

So this is a bad way to learn things, and, importantly, it is bad in one particular direction rather than randomly. All three problems push the same way. Policies get tried where they were most likely to work. Success gets recorded generously. Failures vanish. So the results are not just messy. They are cheerful, and they would stay cheerful even if every policy were useless.

Then there is the one item left on the list, and it is the one that really matters, because no amount of tidier practice could fix it. Laboratory subjects cannot move from one condition to another. People can. A province with a generous benefit attracts the people who need it. A province with a harsh one loses them. So part of what looks like the effect of the policy is really just who moved in and who moved out.

That makes the comparison worse still. But it is also the one thing a laboratory can never give you, because moving house is a verdict delivered by the subjects themselves, and no government department can write it up flatteringly.

So, the author says, we have been defending federalism in the wrong words for two centuries. The point is not that the country finds out what works, because it does not. The point is that when people disagree about something that cannot be settled, they can live under two different answers instead of one, and each side gets its answer without the other having to lose.

That is a real good, and a completely different kind of good. It also fits badly with the first one. The more freely people move to the arrangement that suits them, the better the federation works as a settlement and the worse it works as an experiment. So anybody claiming both at once is claiming more than the arrangement can deliver.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage checks an analogy item by item, which produces three separate charges and a fourth observation, and readers finish holding whichever charge they found most vivid rather than the verdict all four were leading to. The second difficulty is the direction of the error: three defects that all push one way produce a bias, not noise, and that distinction decides the inference question. The third and largest is the fourth paragraph, which takes one fact and uses it against the analogy and then for the passage's own conclusion within four sentences, so a reader tracking the author's attitude registers a reversal that never happened.
mentor.author_intention: To stop the reader defending a political arrangement with an argument that will not survive inspection, and to hand him a different argument for the same arrangement, together with the awkward fact that the two cannot both be pressed at once.

paragraph_journey.note: Let one province try the policy. If it works everyone copies; if it fails only one province pays. A famous and attractive image.
A laboratory gives four things. A federation gives almost none of them: the province chooses, the adopter measures, and failures quietly disappear.
The three faults all push one way, so the results are not messy but cheerful, and would stay cheerful if every policy were useless.
People move between conditions, which ruins the comparison further and at the same time delivers a verdict no laboratory can obtain.
So the case is not knowledge but coexistence: two answers, neither side beaten. And the better that works, the worse the experiment gets.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens generous towards an image it means to inspect, becomes methodical and cool through the checking, sharpens into something close to contempt at the sentence about encouraging results, and then warms in the last two paragraphs as it finds a defence it can keep.
key_transitions: 'Now set the federal case against the list.' (paragraph 2): the analogy stops being admired and starts being tested.
'It is encouraging, and it would go on being encouraging if every one of the policies were worthless.' (end of paragraph 3): the verdict on the arrangement as evidence.
'It is also, at the same time, the one thing in the whole arrangement that a laboratory cannot offer' (paragraph 4): the same fact is turned round and becomes the basis of the defence.
mentor.misunderstanding: The commonest wrong model is that the passage is an attack on federalism, since three of its five paragraphs are spent demolishing the standard argument for it. The author ends by defending the arrangement, on grounds he says are of an entirely different kind. The second wrong model reads the fourth paragraph as a retraction, because it turns appreciative halfway through; the appreciation is for a different property of the same fact, and the criticism is not withdrawn. The third takes the list of defects for the conclusion and misses that the conclusion is about which language the defence should be conducted in.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers one defect as the whole idea, unpredictability where the passage insists on a direction, a retraction where a second use was intended, and a repair or the knowledge defence where the author offers neither. Asking which paragraph an option would let you delete answers three of the four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When a passage builds on an analogy, find the list of things the compared case supplies and check the argument against it item by item, because the author's verdict is nearly always about which items transfer and which do not, and the strongest distractors name a single missing item as the point. The companion habit is to watch for a fact used twice: an author who says a thing is a further wound and at the same time the one thing available elsewhere has not changed his mind, and every option that resolves the pair into praise or blame has lost the argument.
mentor.real_world: The same audit is worth running on any claim that an institution teaches us something by producing variation: pilot schemes inside a company, charter schools, competing regulators, trial sites for a new process. In each, ask who chose to be in the trial, who did the measuring, whether the abandoned attempts were ever written up, and whether the people being studied could leave.
mentor.takeaway: A country of laboratories that never publishes a failure will always look as though its policies work.
mentor.reflection_question: When you last heard that something had been tried successfully somewhere else, who had chosen to try it, and who had counted the result?

eli10.big_idea: Letting provinces differ is a poor way to learn what works but a good way to live with disagreement, and the two clash.
eli10.story: People say provinces are like laboratories: one tries a new policy, others copy it if it works, and only one pays if it fails. But a real lab chooses who gets each treatment, keeps subjects in place, measures fairly and reports failures. Provinces fail three of these tests. They pick policies that suit them, measure their own success and quietly drop failures. All three faults push the same way, so results look cheerful. It is like a cook who shows you only the cakes that rose. The fourth test fails for good: people move to provinces whose rules suit them. That spoils the experiment further. But moving is also an honest vote no lab can get. So the real case is not learning. People who disagree can live under different rules without a fight. The freer people move, the better that works and the worse the experiment.
paragraphs: States the famous idea: provinces are laboratories, so one can try a policy and the rest learn cheaply.
Tests it: a lab gives four things; provinces fail three, since they choose, measure and bury failures themselves.
Names the direction: all three faults make results look good, even if every policy were useless.
Uses one fact twice: people moving spoils the comparison, yet it is a verdict no lab can get.
Moves the defence: provinces let people who disagree each live under their own answer, which clashes with learning.
eli10.author_view: The writer is cool and sceptical about the laboratory image, but warms to federalism once it is defended for the right reason.
